questions.q: Why did the woman whose son Elisha restored to life live in the land of the Philistines seven years?
questions.a: The woman whose son Elisha restored to life lived in the land of the Philistines seven years because Elisha said Yahweh had called for a famine.

questions.q: Why did the woman go to the king?
questions.a: The woman went to the king to beg him for her house and for her land.

questions.q: What was Gehazi telling the king when the woman whose son Elisha restored to life arrived?
questions.a: Gehazi was telling the king how Elisha had restored to life the child who was dead.

questions.q: What did Hazael take with him to give to Elisha?
questions.a: Hazael took a gift with him of every kind of good thing of Damascus, carried by forty camels.

questions.q: Why did the man of God weep?
questions.a: The man of God wept because he knew the evil that Hazael would do to the people of Israel.

questions.q: After Hazael told the king of Aram that he would recover, what did he do to King Ben Hadad?
questions.a: After Hazael told King Ben Hadad that he would recover, he took the blanket and dipped it in water, and spread it on Ben Hadad’s face so that he died.

questions.q: Why was Yahweh not willing to destroy Judah?
questions.a: Yahweh was unwilling to destroy Judah because he had told his servant David that his descendants would always be kings.

questions.q: When did Edom revolt from under the hand of Judah?
questions.a: In Jehoram’s days, Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah.

questions.q: Why did Ahaziah do what was evil in Yahweh’s sight?
questions.a: Ahaziah did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight, for Ahaziah was a son-in-law to the house of Ahab.

questions.q: Where did King Joram return to be healed of the wounds that the Arameans had given him at Ramah?
questions.a: King Joram returned to be healed in Jezreel.

commentary.text: A famine in Israel, The Shunammite obtains her land.
Elisha consulted by Hazael, Death of Benhadad.

Verses 1–6 The kindness of the good Shunammite to Elisha, was rewarded by the care taken of her in famine. It is well to foresee an evil, and wisdom, when we foresee it, to hide ourselves if we lawfully may do so. When the famine was over, she returned out of the land of the Philistines; that was no proper place for an Israelite, any longer than there was necessity for it. Time was when she dwelt so securely among her own people, that she had no occasion to be spoken for to the king; but there is much uncertainty in this life, so that things or persons may fail us which we most depend upon, and those befriend us which we think we shall never need. Sometimes events, small in themselves, prove of consequence, as here; for they made the king ready to believe Gehazi's narrative, when thus confirmed. It made him ready to grant her request, and to support a life which was given once and again by miracle.

Among other changes of men's minds by affliction, it often gives other thoughts of God's ministers, and teaches to value the counsels and prayers of those whom they have hated and despised. It was not in Hazael's countenance that Elisha read what he would do, but God revealed it to him, and it fetched tears from his eyes: the more foresight men have, the more grief they are liable to. It is possible for a man, under the convictions and restraints of natural conscience, to express great abhorrence of a sin, yet afterwards to be reconciled to it. Those that are little and low in the world, cannot imagine how strong the temptations of power and prosperity are, which, if ever they arrive at, they will find how deceitful their hearts are, how much worse than they suspected. The devil ruins men, by saying they shall certainly recover and do well, so rocking them asleep in security. Hazael's false account was an injury to the king, who lost the benefit of the prophet's warning to prepare for death, and an injury to Elisha, who would be counted a false prophet. It is not certain that Hazael murdered his master, or if he caused his death it may have been without any design. But he was a dissembler, and afterwards proved a persecutor to Israel.

A general idea is given of Jehoram's badness. His father, no doubt, had him taught the true knowledge of the Lord, but did ill to marry him to the daughter of Ahab; no good could come of union with an idolatrous family.

Names do not make natures, but it was bad for Jehoshaphat's family to borrow names from Ahab's. Ahaziah's relation to Ahab's family was the occasion of his wickedness and of his fall. When men choose wives for themselves, let them remember they are choosing mothers for their children. Providence so ordered it, that Ahaziah might be cut off with the house of Ahab, when the measure of their iniquity was full. Those who partake with sinners in their sin, must expect to partake with them in their plagues. May all the changes, troubles, and wickedness of the world, make us more earnest to obtain an interest in the salvation of Christ.
